Question 1 (0625/42_Summer_2017_Q5) - Thermal Effects, Electricity

(a) (i) An electric kettle contains 600g of water at 20°C. The heater in the kettle operates at 240 V. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200J/(kg°C). The current in the heater is 12 A. Calculate the time taken for the temperature of the water to rise to 100°C. [4]

Tap to reveal answer
First, calculate the thermal energy required: E = mcΔT.
E = 0.6 kg × 4200 J/(kg°C) × (100°C - 20°C) = 201600 J.
Next, calculate the electrical energy supplied per second (power): P = VI.
P = 240 V × 12 A = 2880 W.
Finally, calculate the time: time = E⁄P = 201600 J⁄2880 W = 70 s.

(ii) State one assumption you made in your calculation in calculation in (a)(i). [1]

Tap to reveal answer
The assumption made is that there are no thermal energy losses to the surroundings.

(b) Using the apparatus shown in Fig. 5.1, describe an experiment to demonstrate good and bad emitters of thermal radiation. Include the expected results and the conclusion. You may use a diagram. [4]

Tap to reveal answer
First, fill the metal bottle with hot water. Then, place the two thermometers at equal distances from the black and white sides of the bottle. Record the temperature readings from both thermometers at regular intervals.
Expected result: The thermometer near the black side will show a higher temperature reading or its temperature will rise faster.
Conclusion: This demonstrates that black surfaces are better emitters of thermal radiation than white surfaces.
Question 2 (0625/42_Summer_2017_Q8) - Electricity, Electron And Electronics

Fig. 8.1 shows a 12.0V power supply connected in a circuit.

The circuit includes a lamp and a resistance wire AB of constant cross-sectional area. There is a sliding contact that can be moved between A and B.

(a) The rating of the lamp at normal brightness is 6.0V, 9.0W. Calculate

(i) the current in the lamp at normal brightness, [2]

Tap to reveal answer
Using the formula P = VI, the current I = P⁄V = 9.0W⁄6.0V = 1.5 A.

(ii) the resistance of the lamp at norma normal brightness. [2]

Tap to reveal answer
Using Ohm's Law, R = V⁄I = 6.0V⁄1.5A = 4.0 Ω.

(b) AB is 1.00 m long and has a resistance of 5.0Ω. The lamp has normal brightness when the sliding contact is at X.

(i) The sliding contact is moved to B. Explain, without a calculation, why the lamp becomes dimmer.

Tap to reveal answer
When the contact is moved to B, the length of the resistance wire in the circuit increases. This means the total resistance of the circuit is greater, which causes the current to decrease and the lamp to become dimmer.

(ii) Calculate the distance AX for the lamp to have normal brightness. [3]

Tap to reveal answer
For the lamp to have normal brightness, the p.d. across it must be 6.0V. The total p.d. is 12.0V, so the p.d. across the wire section AX must also be 6.0V.
The current at normal brightness is 1.5A. The resistance of wire AX is R = V⁄I = 6.0V⁄1.5A = 4.0 Ω.
Since the 1.00m wire has a total resistance of 5.0Ω, the distance AX is (4.0Ω⁄5.0Ω) × 1.00 m = 0.80 m.
Question 3 (0625/41_Summer_2017_Q9) - Electricity, Electron And Electronics

(a) The resistance of a circuit component varies with the brightness of the light falling on its surface.

(i) State the name of the component. [1]

Tap to reveal answer
LDR or light-dependent resistor.

(ii) Draw the circuit symbol for this component. [1]

(b) Fig. 9.1 shows a 6.0V battery connected in series with a 1.2kΩ resistor and a thermistor.

(i) At a certain temperature, the resistance of the thermistor is 2.4 kΩ. Calculate the reading on the voltmeter. [4]

Tap to reveal answer
This is a potential divider circuit. The total resistance is 1.2 kΩ + 2.4 kΩ = 3.6 kΩ.
The voltmeter reads the p.d. across the thermistor.
Vout = (Rthermistor⁄Rtotal) × Vin = (2.4 kΩ⁄3.6 kΩ) × 6.0 V = 4.0 V.

(ii) The battery connected to the circuit in Fig. 9.1 is not changed. Suggest a change that would cause the reading of the voltmeter to decrease. [1]

Tap to reveal answer
To decrease the voltmeter reading (the p.d. across the thermistor), you could increase the temperature, which would decrease the thermistor's resistance.
Question 4 (0625/43_Summer_2017_Q9) - Electricity, Electron And Electronics

A 12V battery is connected in series to a 24W lamp and to a parallel pair of identical resistors X and Y. Fig. 9.1 is the circuit diagram.

The 24 W lamp lights at normal brightness when the potential difference (p.d.) across it is 6.0V. The lamp is at normal brightness.

(a) Calculate the resistance of the lamp. [3]

Tap to reveal answer
First, find the current: I = P⁄V = 24W⁄6.0V = 4.0 A.
Then, find the resistance: R = V⁄I = 6.0V⁄4.0A = 1.5 Ω.

(b) Determine

(i) the p.d. between A and B, [1]

Tap to reveal answer
The total voltage is 12V and the lamp uses 6.0V, so the remaining voltage is across the parallel pair AB.
p.d. = 12V - 6.0V = 6.0 V.

(ii) the combined resistance of the parallel pair of identical resistors X and Y, [1]

Tap to reveal answer
The total current of 4.0A flows through the parallel pair. The p.d. is 6.0V.
R = V⁄I = 6.0V⁄4.0A = 1.5 Ω.

(iii) the resistance of X. [2]

Tap to reveal answer
For two identical resistors in parallel, the combined resistance is half the individual resistance.
So, the resistance of X is 1.5 Ω × 2 = 3.0 Ω.

(c) Resistor X is removed from the circuit in Fig 9.1. Explain why the lamp becomes dimmer.

Tap to reveal answer
When X is removed, the resistance of that part of the circuit increases from 1.5Ω to 3.0Ω. This increases the total resistance of the circuit. A higher total resistance causes the current in the lamp to decrease, making it dimmer.
Question 5 (0625/41_Summer_2017_Q10) - Electricity

(a) Describe the movement of charge that causes an object to become positively charged. [1]

Tap to reveal answer
Electrons / negative charges are removed from the object.

(b) Fig. 10.1 shows a negatively charged rod held over an uncharged metal sphere.

(i) On Fig. 10.1, add + and - signs to represent the results of the movement of charge within the sphere. [2]

(ii) Describe the actions that must be taken to obtain an even distribution of positive charge on the surface of the sphere. [2]

Tap to reveal answer
While the negatively charged rod is held nearby, connect an earth wire to the sphere. This allows electrons to be repelled from the sphere and flow to the earth. Then, remove the earth wire first, and finally, remove the charged rod. The excess positive charge will then distribute evenly over the sphere.
Question 6 (0625/42_Winter_2017_Q8) - Electricity

Fig. 8.1 is a circuit diagram.

Calculate

(a) the resistance of the circuit, [4]

Tap to reveal answer
First, calculate the resistance of the series part: 8.0Ω + 4.0Ω = 12.0Ω.
Next, calculate the total resistance of the two parallel branches:
1⁄Rtotal = 1⁄12Ω + 1⁄6.0Ω = 1+2⁄12Ω = 3⁄12Ω.
Rtotal = 12⁄3 = 4.0 Ω.

(b) the potential difference (p.d.) across the 8.0Ω resistor. [2]

Tap to reveal answer
The total p.d. across the top branch is 24V. The current in the top branch is I = V⁄R = 24V⁄12Ω = 2.0A.
The p.d. across the 8.0Ω resistor is V = IR = 2.0A × 8.0Ω = 16 V.
Question 7 (0625/43_Winter_2017_Q8) - Electricity

(a) Fig. 8.1 shows an uncharged conducting sphere on an insulating stand placed close to a positively charged rod. The rod and the sphere are not moved.

Describe how to charge the sphere using a wire connected to earth and explain whether the sphere becomes positively charged or negatively charged. [3]

Tap to reveal answer
First, touch the sphere with the earth wire. Since the rod is positive, electrons are attracted by the positive rod and flow from the earth to the sphere. Then, remove the earth wire before removing the rod. The sphere becomes negatively charged.

(b) Fig. 8.2 shows a small black circle that represents a positive charge.

On Fig. 8.2. draw the pattern and the direction of the electric field in the region around the charge. [2]

(c) A charge of 7.0C flows along a wire in 5.0 minutes. Calculate the current in the wire. [2]

Tap to reveal answer
Time in seconds = 5.0 min × 60 s/min = 300 s.
Current I = Q⁄t = 7.0C⁄300s = 0.023 A.
Question 8 (0625/41_Winter_2017_Q9) - Electricity

Fig. 9.1 shows a circuit with three 1.5 V cells.

(a) Calculate

(i) the total electromotive force (e.m.f.) of the cells, [1]

Tap to reveal answer
e.m.f. = 3 × 1.5 V = 4.5 V.

(ii) the total resistance of the circuit, [3]

Tap to reveal answer
The resistors are in parallel. 1⁄Rtotal = 1⁄3.0Ω + 1⁄6.0Ω = 2+1⁄6.0Ω = 3⁄6.0Ω.
Rtotal = 6.0⁄3 = 2.0 Ω.

(iii) the current in the 3.0Ω resistor. [2]

Tap to reveal answer
The p.d. across the parallel branch is 4.5V.
I = V⁄R = 4.5V⁄3.0Ω = 1.5 A.

(b) State, using the letters in Fig. 9.1, how you would connect

(i) an ammeter to measure the total current in the circuit, [1]

Tap to reveal answer
Connect the ammeter in series, either between A and B or between G and H.

(ii) a voltmeter to measure the potential difference (p.d.) across the 6.0Ω resistor. [1]

Tap to reveal answer
Connect the voltmeter in parallel, with its terminals connected to points E and F.

IGCSE Physics - Chapter 8: Electricity (9-16)

Question 9 (0625/41_Summer_2018_Q7) - Electricity

(a) State, in terms of their structure, why metals are good conductors of electricity. [1]

Tap to reveal answer
Metals contain free/mobile electrons (or delocalised electrons) that are able to move through the structure and carry charge.

(b) A cylindrical metal wire W₁ of length l and cross-sectional area A, has a resistance of 16Ω. A second cylindrical wire W₂ having length l⁄2 and cross-sectional area 2A, is made from the same metal. Determine

(i) the resistance of W₂, [2]

Tap to reveal answer
Resistance is proportional to length and inversely proportional to area. Halving the length halves the resistance (16Ω → 8Ω). Doubling the area also halves the resistance (8Ω → 4Ω).
So, the new resistance is 16Ω × (1⁄2) × (1⁄2) = 4.0 Ω.

(ii) the effective resistance of W₁ and W₂ when connected in parallel. [2]

Tap to reveal answer
Using the formula for parallel resistors: 1⁄Rp = 1⁄R₁ + 1⁄R₂ = 1⁄16Ω + 1⁄4Ω = 1+4⁄16Ω = 5⁄16Ω.
Rp = 16⁄5 = 3.2 Ω.

(c) The parallel pair of resistors in (b)(ii) is connected to a battery that is made from three cells in series, each of electromotive force (e.m.f.) E. There is a current in each resistor.

(i) State the e.m.f. of the battery. [1]

Tap to reveal answer
The e.m.f. of the battery is 3E.

(ii) The current in the battery is IB, the current in W₁ is I₁ and the current in W₂ is I₂. Place a tick (✓) in one box to indicate how these three currents are related. [1]

Tap to reveal answer
The correct box is IB > I₂ > I₁.
Question 10 (0625/42_Summer_2018_Q8) - Electricity, Electron And Electronics

Fig. 8.1 shows a circuit that contains a battery of electromotive force (e.m.f.) 6.0V, an ammeter, a 20Ω resistor and component X.

(a) (i) State the name of component X. [1]

Tap to reveal answer
Component X is a variable resistor or rheostat.

(ii) The potential difference (p.d.) across the 20Ω resistor is measured with a voltmeter. On Fig. 8.1, draw the symbol for this voltmeter connected to the circuit. [1]

(b) The p.d. across the 20Ω resistor is varied from zero to 6.0V. For each value of p.d. a corresponding current is measured. On Fig. 8.2, draw a line to indicate how the current measured by the ammeter depends on the p.d. across the 20Ω resistor. [3]

(c) A second resistor is connected into the circuit in parallel with the 20Ω resistor.

(i) State how the combined resistance of the two resistors in parallel compares with the resistance of each of the resistors on its own. [1]

Tap to reveal answer
The combined resistance is less than the resistance of either resistor on its own.

(ii) The p.d. across the two parallel resistors is changed and the current in the battery for each value of the p.d. is measured. A second line could be drawn on Fig. 8.2 to indicate how the current measured by the am ammeter depends on the p.d. across the two resistors in parallel. State how the second line differs from the original line. You are not expected to draw this second line. [1]

Tap to reveal answer
The second line would be steeper (have a greater gradient) than the original line.
Question 11 (0625/43_Summer_2018_Q9) - Electricity

Fig. 9.1 shows a circuit that includes a battery of electromotive force (e.m.f.) 12V.

The reading on the ammeter is 0.15A.

(a) Calculate the resistance of the circuit. [2]

Tap to reveal answer
Using Ohm's Law for the whole circuit, R = V⁄I = 12V⁄0.15A = 80 Ω.

(b) The variable resistor is adjusted so that its resistance decreases.

(i) State what happens to the reading on the ammeter. [1]

Tap to reveal answer
The reading on the ammeter increases.

(ii) State and explain what happens to the reading on the voltmeter. [2]

Tap to reveal answer
The reading on the voltmeter decreases. The voltmeter is measuring the p.d. across the variable resistor. Since its resistance has decreased and the current has increased, a larger share of the total voltage is now across the fixed 20Ω resistor, leaving less for the variable resistor.

(c) The battery is formed from cells of electromotive force (e.m.f.) 1.5 V.

(i) Explain, in terms of electrical energy, what is meant by an electromotive force (e.m.f.) of 1.5 V. [2]

Tap to reveal answer
An e.m.f. of 1.5V means that the cell supplies 1.5 Joules of electrical energy for every coulomb of charge that passes through it.

(ii) State how many 1.5 V cells are connected in series to form the battery. [1]

Tap to reveal answer
Number of cells = Total e.m.f.⁄e.m.f. per cell = 12V⁄1.5V = 8 cells.
Question 12 (0625/42_Summer_2018_Q10) - Electricity

(a) An uncharged conducting metal plate rests on insulating supports. Fig. 10.1 shows the plate and a positively charged insulating plastic sheet placed on top of the metal plate.

(i) Describe any flow of charge that takes place when the plastic sheet is placed onto the metal plate. [1]

Tap to reveal answer
Electrons (negative charges) within the metal plate are attracted to the positive plastic sheet and move towards the top surface of the plate.

(ii) On Fig. 10.1, draw how charges are now arranged within the metal plate. [1]

(iii) State and explain if this arrangement of charge helps to keep the plastic sheet in place. [2]

Tap to reveal answer
Yes, it helps keep the plastic sheet in place. The accumulation of negative charges on the top surface of the metal plate and positive charges on the bottom creates an electrostatic attraction. The unlike charges attract, so there is an attractive force between the metal plate and the plastic sheet.

(b) Fig. 10.2 shows two uncharged conducting spheres suspended on insulating threads.

1. The spheres are now both given positive charges. On Fig. 10.2, draw a possible position of each sphere and thread.

2. Explain the positions you have drawn. [2]

Tap to reveal answer
The spheres will move apart from each other, with the threads angled outwards. This is because both spheres have positive charges, and like charges repel.
Question 13 (0625/42_Winter_2018_Q7) - Electricity

Fig. 7.1 shows three identical lamps and an ammeter connected to a power supply.

The switches are closed. Each lamp is rated at 60 W and operates at its normal working voltage of 110V.

(a) Calculate:

(i) the current in each lamp [2]

Tap to reveal answer
Using P = VI, the current I = P⁄V = 60W⁄110V = 0.55 A.

(ii) the current in the ammeter [1]

Tap to reveal answer
The lamps are in parallel, so the total current is the sum of the currents in each branch.
Total current = 3 × 0.55 A = 1.6 A.

(iii) the voltage of the power supply. [1]

Tap to reveal answer
In a parallel circuit, the voltage across each branch is the same as the supply voltage, so it is 110 V.

(b) (i) Calculate the resistance of the filament of one of the lamps when working normally. [2]

Tap to reveal answer
Using Ohm's Law, R = V⁄I = 110V⁄0.55A = 200 Ω.

(ii) Another lamp X has a filament with twice the resistance of each lamp in the circuit of Fig. 7.1. The material and the temperature of the filament in lamp X is the same as the filaments in the lamps in Fig. 7.1. In Table 7.1, tick any box in the right-hand column that shows a possible difference between the filament of lamp X and a filament of one of the lamps in the circuit. [2]

Tap to reveal answer
To get twice the resistance with the same material, you can either have twice the length or half the area of cross-section.
Question 14 (0625/43_Winter_2018_Q7) - Electricity

A defibrillator is a machine that sends an electrical charge through the heart of a patient whose heart is not beating correctly. Doctors learn to use a defibrillator by practising on a medical dummy. Fig. 7.1 shows the two contacts of a defibrillator attached to a medical dummy.

The contacts that touch the dummy are made from metal, and when the defibrillator is being used, one contact becomes strongly negatively charged and the other contact becomes strongly positively charged. The handles of the contacts are made from plastic, which is an electrical insulator.

(a) (i) State how the structure of an electrical insulator differs from the structure of a conductor. [1]

Tap to reveal answer
An insulator has no free/delocalised electrons, whereas a conductor does.

(ii) Suggest why the handles are made from an electrical insulator. [2]

Tap to reveal answer
The handles are made from an insulator to prevent charge from flowing through the doctor, ensuring the doctor does not get an electric shock which could be fatal or cause injury.

(b) Explain, in terms of the particles involved, how one contact becomes negatively charged and how the other contact becomes comes positively charged. [2]

Tap to reveal answer
Electrons move from one contact to the other. The contact that gains electrons becomes negatively charged, and the contact that loses electrons becomes positively charged.

(c) The defibrillator passes a charge of 9.1 × 10⁻³ C through the medical dummy in 6.5 × 10⁻⁴ s. Calculate the average current in the dummy. [2]

Tap to reveal answer
Using the formula I = Q⁄t = 9.1 × 10⁻³ C⁄6.5 × 10⁻⁴ s = 14 A.
Question 15 (0625/42_Winter_2018_Q8) - Electricity

(a) (i) Fig. 8.1 shows a positively charged cube of insulating material. The cube is fixed to a piece of wood that is floating on water. A negatively charged rod is held above the piece of wood and brought close to the cube, as shown.

State and explain any movement of the piece of wood. [2]

Tap to reveal answer
The piece of wood moves towards the negative rod. This is because opposite charges attract.

(ii) Fig. 8.2 shows two cubes of insulating material. One is positively charged and the other is negatively charged. The cubes are fixed to a piece of wood that is floating on water. Charged rods are held above the piece of wood and brought close to the cubes, as shown.

State and explain any movement of the piece of wood. [2]

Tap to reveal answer
The piece of wood rotates/turns. The attractive force on the positive cube and the repulsive force on the negative cube create a turning effect (a couple).

(b) In terms of a simple electron model, describe the differences between conductors and insulators. [2]

Tap to reveal answer
Conductors: Contain free/delocalised electrons that are able to move and carry charge.
Insulators: Electrons are fixed in place and cannot move freely.

(c) On Fig. 8.3, draw the electric field pattern around a single point positive charge. [1]

Question 16 (0625/43_Winter_2018_Q8) - Electricity

A 9.0V battery is connected to a 120Ω resistor in series with wire P. Fig. 8.1 shows a voltmeter connected across the 120Ω resistor.

(a) State the energy changes that are taking place in the circuit. [2]

Tap to reveal answer
Chemical energy in the battery is converted to electrical energy, which is then converted to thermal energy (heat) in the resistors.

(b) The reading on the voltmeter is 2.4 V. Calculate:

(i) the current in the 120Ω resistor [2]

Tap to reveal answer
Using Ohm's Law, I = V⁄R = 2.4V⁄120Ω = 0.020 A.

(ii) the potential difference (p.d.) across wire P [1]

Tap to reveal answer
The total p.d. is 9.0V. The p.d. across P is 9.0V - 2.4V = 6.6 V.

(iii) the resistance of wire P [1]

Tap to reveal answer
The current is the same (0.020A). Using Ohm's Law, R = V⁄I = 6.6V⁄0.020A = 330 Ω.

(c) Wire P has a diameter d and a length L. A second piece of wire Q is made of the same material. The diameter of wire Q is 0.50 × d and its length is 5.0 × L. Calculate the resistance of wire Q. [4]

Tap to reveal answer
Resistance is proportional to length (L) and inversely proportional to area (A), and A is proportional to d².
Effect of length: 5.0 × L means resistance is multiplied by 5.
Effect of diameter: 0.50 × d means area is multiplied by (0.5)² = 0.25. Since R ∝ 1/A, resistance is multiplied by 1/0.25 = 4.
New resistance = 330Ω × 5 × 4 = 6600 Ω.

Question 17 (0625/41_Winter_2018_Q9) - Electricity

Fig. 9.1 shows the symbol for a 12 V battery.

(a) Two lamps are connected in parallel with the battery. On Fig. 9.1, using the correct symbols, complete the circuit diagram. [1]

(b) One of these lamps has a resistance of 6.0Ω. Calculate, for this lamp:

(i) the current [1]

Tap to reveal answer
Using Ohm's Law, I = V⁄R = 12 V⁄6.0 Ω = 2.0 A.

(ii) the power. [2]

Tap to reveal answer
Using the formula P = VI = 12 V × 2.0 A = 24 W.

(c) The power of the other lamp is 36 W. Calculate the total energy delivered to this lamp in 20 hours. [3]

Tap to reveal answer

Question 18 (0625/43_Winter_2018_Q9) - Electricity, Magnets And Currents

(a) Describe how a direct current (d.c.) differs from an alternating current (a.c.). [1]

Tap to reveal answer
A direct current (d.c.) flows in only one direction and has a constant value, while an alternating current (a.c.) continuously changes direction.

(b) Fig. 9.1 shows how the voltage output of an a.c. generator varies with time.

A heater is connected directly to the a.c. generator and the maximum current in the heater is 0.75A.

(i) On Fig. 9.2, sketch a graph to indicate how the current in the heater varies with time. [1]

(ii) Calculate the power produced by the heater when the current is 0.75A. [2]

Tap to reveal answer
From the voltage graph (Fig 9.1), the maximum voltage is 7.2V. When the current is at its maximum of 0.75A, the voltage is also at its maximum.
Using P = VI = 7.2 V × 0.75 A = 5.4 W.

(c) Fig. 9.3 shows the coil ABCD of the a.c. generator between two magnetic poles.

(i) On Fig. 9.3, draw a straight arrow to indicate the direction in which side AB of the coil is moving. Label this arrow M. [1]

(ii) Deduce the direction of the current induced in side AB of the coil and explain your reasoning. [2]

Tap to reveal answer
The current is from A to B. This can be determined using Fleming's Right-Hand Rule, where the thumb points in the direction of motion (upwards), the first finger points in the direction of the magnetic field (N to S), and the second finger indicates the direction of the induced current.

(iii) The rate at which the coil of the a.c. generator rotates increases. State two ways in which the alternating voltage changes. [2]

Tap to reveal answer
1. The maximum voltage (amplitude) becomes greater.
2. The frequency increases (or the time period decreases).
Question 19 (0625/42_Summer_2019_Q3) - Forces And Energy, Electricity

Fig. 3.1 shows solar cells used to generate electrical energy.

(a) State the main form of energy transferred from the Sun to the solar cells for the generation of electrical energy. [1]

Tap to reveal answer
Light energy.

(b) Consider the generation of electrical energy by a large number of solar cells, as shown in Fig. 3.1.

(i) State one environmental advantage and one environmental disadvantage. [2]

Tap to reveal answer
Advantage: It produces no air pollution or greenhouse gases during operation.
Disadvantage: It can cause visual pollution or requires a large area of land.

(ii) State and explain whether this source of electrical energy is renewable. [1]

Tap to reveal answer
Yes, it is renewable because the energy source (the Sun) is not used up in the process.

(c) Each group of solar cells is arranged in a rectangle 1.2 m × 2.8 m. The solar cells are situated in a region where 260W of solar energy is received per square metre of the cells. The electrical output of each group of solar cells is a current of 2.5 A with a potential difference of 86 V. Calculate the efficiency of the solar cells. [4]

Tap to reveal answer
First, calculate the power input: Area = 1.2m × 2.8m = 3.36 m².
Power Input = 260 W/m² × 3.36 m² = 874 W.
Next, calculate the power output: P = VI = 86 V × 2.5 A = 215 W.
Efficiency = (Power Output⁄Power Input) × 100% = (215W⁄874W) × 100% = 25%.
Question 20 (0625/41_Summer_2019_Q7) - Electricity

Fig. 7.1 shows a circuit diagram that includes component X.

(a) State the name of component X. [1]

Tap to reveal answer
Component X is a thermistor.

(b) The electromotive force (e.m.f.) of the battery is E. The switch is closed. The potential difference (p.d.) across the 30Ω resistor is V₃₀. The p.d. across the 20Ω resistor is V₂₀. The p.d. across component X is Vₓ. State an equation that relates Vₓ to:

(i) V₃₀ [1]

Tap to reveal answer
Vₓ = V₃₀

(ii) E and V₂₀. [1]

Tap to reveal answer
Vₓ = E - V₂₀

(c) The e.m.f. of the battery is 6.0V and the resistance of component X is 15Ω. Calculate:

(i) the total resistance of the circuit [3]

Tap to reveal answer
First find the resistance of the parallel part: 1⁄Rp = 1⁄15Ω + 1⁄30Ω = 2+1⁄30Ω. So, Rp = 10Ω.
Total resistance = Rp + 20Ω = 10Ω + 20Ω = 30 Ω.

(ii) the ammeter reading. [2]

Tap to reveal answer
Using Ohm's Law, I = V⁄Rtotal = 6.0V⁄30Ω = 0.20 A.

(d) The temperature of component X increases. State and explain what happens to the ammeter reading. [2]

Tap to reveal answer
When the temperature of the thermistor (X) increases, its resistance decreases. This causes the total resistance of the circuit to decrease. As a result, the ammeter reading (total current) increases.
Question 21 (0625/42_Summer_2019_Q8) - Electricity, Electron And Electronics

(a) A conducting sphere is mounted on an insulating stand. Explain how you would use a positively charged rod of insulating material to charge the sphere by induction. [3]

Tap to reveal answer
1. Bring the positively charged rod close to the sphere, but do not touch it.

Fuse rating: 13 A.

A thicker wire has a lower resistance. For a given current, a lower resistance means less heating effect (P=I²R). Therefore, a thicker wire can carry a higher current before it gets hot enough to melt.

Tap to reveal answer

Next, calculate the temperature change: ΔT = 35°C - 16°C = 19°C.

Question 27 (0625/42_Winter_2019_Q7) - Electricity, Magnets And Currents

(a) Fig. 7.1 shows a coil of wire wound on a thin plastic cylinder. The plastic has no effect on any magnetic field. The galvanometer is extremely sensitive.

Tap to reveal answer
A deflection is observed on the galvanometer, which then returns to zero and deflects in the opposite direction as the magnet leaves the coil. This happens because as the magnet moves through the coil, the magnetic field lines cut the coil, inducing an e.m.f. and causing a current to flow.

Tap to reveal answer
A larger deflection is observed. Releasing from point B, a greater height, means the trolley has a higher speed as it passes through the coil. This causes a larger rate of change of magnetic flux, which induces a larger e.m.f. and current.

Question 31 (0625/43_Winter_2019_Q9) - Electricity, Electron And Electronics

Fig. 9.1 shows a circuit containing an LED and two resistors in parallel, each of resistance R. The normal operating voltage of the LED is 2.1 V and the normal current is 0.19A.

(a) (i) The potential difference (p.d.) across the LED is measured with a voltmeter. On Fig. 9.1, draw the symbol for this voltmeter connected to the circuit. [1]

(ii) The current in the LED is measured with an ammeter. On Fig. 9.1, draw the symbol for this ammeter connected to the circuit. [1]

(b) Calculate the value of R when the LED is operating normally. [5]

Tap to reveal answer
The circuit consists of the parallel resistor pair in series with the LED.
The total voltage is 3.7V. The voltage across the LED is 2.1V.
Therefore, the voltage across the parallel resistor pair is 3.7V - 2.1V = 1.6V.

The total current flowing through the series circuit is the same as the current in the LED, which is 0.19A.
The combined resistance of the parallel pair can be calculated using Ohm's Law:
Rparallel = V⁄I = 1.6V⁄0.19A = 8.42 Ω.

For two identical resistors R in parallel, the combined resistance is Rparallel = R⁄2.
So, R = 2 × Rparallel = 2 × 8.42 Ω = 17 Ω.
Question 32 (0625/41_Summer_2020_Q8) - Electricity

The power supply used in an electric vehicle contains 990 rechargeable cells each of electromotive force (e.m.f.) 1.2V. The cells are contained in packs in which all the cells are in series with each other. The e.m.f. of each pack is 54 V.

(a) Calculate the number of packs in the power supply. [2]

Tap to reveal answer
First, find the number of cells in one pack:
Number of cells per pack = e.m.f. of pack⁄e.m.f. of cell = 54 V⁄1.2 V = 45 cells.

Now, find the total number of packs:
Number of packs = Total number of cells⁄Cells per pack = 990⁄45 = 22 packs.

(b) When in use, each pack supplies a current of 3.5 A.

(i) Calculate the rate at which each cell is transferring chemical energy to electrical energy. [2]

Tap to reveal answer
The rate of energy transfer is power. For one cell, P = EI (using e.m.f. as it's the source).
Power = 1.2 V × 3.5 A = 4.2 W.

(ii) The packs are connected in parallel to supply a large current to drive the electric vehicle. Explain why it is necessary to use thick wires to carry this current. [3]

Tap to reveal answer
A large total current flows from the parallel packs. Thick wires have a smaller resistance. A lower resistance reduces the amount of thermal energy generated in the wires (since heat loss is proportional to I²R). This improves efficiency and prevents the wires from overheating or melting.

(b) Fig. 8.1 shows a polystyrene ball covered with aluminium paint. The polystyrene ball is suspended between two charged metal plates by an insulated thread. The ball oscillates between the two charged plates. Explain why the ball oscillates. [4]

Space for diagram Fig. 8.1
Tap to reveal answer
1. The uncharged conducting ball is initially attracted to one of the plates (e.g., the positive plate).
2. When it touches the positive plate, it transfers electrons to the plate and becomes positively charged itself.
3. Now being positively charged, it is repelled by the positive plate and attracted to the negative plate.
4. It moves across and touches the negative plate, where it gains electrons and becomes negatively charged.
5. Now negatively charged, it is repelled by the negative plate and attracted back to the positive plate. This process repeats, causing the oscillation.

Resistance R is proportional to length L (R ∝ L) and inversely proportional to cross-sectional area A (R ∝ 1⁄A). Area is proportional to the square of the diameter (A ∝ d²).
The new wire has twice the length, which doubles the resistance.
It also has twice the diameter, which means the area is 2² = 4 times larger. This decreases the resistance by a factor of 4.
New Resistance = R × 2 × (1⁄4) = R × 0.5 = 2.3 Ω × 0.5 = 1.1 Ω.
